messages.text: I’m just so tired of everything. It feels like I’m running on empty and there’s no point in refilling.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying a lot for a long time, and that exhaustion feels overwhelming. When you say there’s “no point,” do you mean you’re feeling hopeless about things improving? I want to understand how deep this fatigue goes for you so we can explore what might help. Are you also feeling emotionally drained, or is it more physical?
The future just feels like more of the same. I don’t see anything changing, and honestly, I don’t know if I care anymore.

That sense of numbness and hopelessness can be really heavy, and it often makes it difficult to imagine any reason to keep going. Sometimes these feelings can also point toward thoughts of not wanting to be alive—are you experiencing anything like that? It’s important to know so we can keep you safe and support you appropriately. Would you feel comfortable telling me if you’ve had thoughts of harming yourself?
I wouldn’t say I’m thinking about harming myself. I just… wouldn’t mind if I didn’t wake up, you know? It’s not dramatic—it’s just how it is.

I hear you saying it’s not about actively doing something, but that there’s a sense of indifference toward being alive, which is still important to take seriously. Those thoughts can be a sign that you’re under immense strain and could use extra support right now. Would you be willing to talk about what’s been going on recently that’s brought you to this point? We can look at ways to make the load feel a bit lighter.
It’s just… I never thought I’d outlive her. And now the house feels full, but I’ve never felt more alone. The kids are here, but they don’t see me—I’m just the guy paying the bills.

It sounds like losing her has left you with a deep absence that no amount of noise or activity can fill, and that disconnection from your kids adds to the isolation. Grief can make it hard to feel seen, even by those closest to you. Would it be okay if we explored ways to reconnect with them emotionally and also carve out spaces where you can share your loss openly? You don’t have to carry this alone.
I should be able to handle this on my own. I’m a grown man, a professional—I’ve helped others through worse. It’s pathetic that I can’t just pull myself together.

It’s not pathetic—it’s human. Grief and loneliness can overwhelm even the most capable people, and needing support doesn’t diminish your strength or professionalism. Sometimes the resilience we offer others needs to be turned inward and shared with ourselves. What would it feel like to let someone help you, just for now?
Part of me wants to let someone in, but I just don’t want to be a burden. I’ve always been the one others lean on—it feels wrong to ask for help now.

Feeling like a burden is a common worry, but often those who care about you want the chance to support you just as you’ve supported them. Sharing what you’re carrying can deepen relationships rather than weaken them. If you imagine telling someone close what’s really on your mind, who might that be? We can think together about how to start that conversation gently.
I don’t know… maybe my sister. But she’s got her own life. Anyway, I’m not even sure what I’d say. “Sorry I’m sad again”? It’s not exactly conversation starter material.

You don’t have to find the perfect words—sometimes starting with something simple like “I’ve been having a tough time lately” is enough to open the door. People who care about you often want to know what’s really going on, even if it’s messy. We could work on a few sentences that feel safe and honest without overwhelming either of you. Would you like to try that together?
I appreciate the idea, but I’m not ready to say those words out loud yet. Maybe later.

That’s completely okay—this is your pace, and there’s no rush. Even just acknowledging the thought of sharing is a meaningful step. In the meantime, we can focus on small ways to lighten the weight you’re carrying. Would you like to explore coping strategies you can try on your own for now?
Is it okay to just… take small steps? I don’t know if I can handle big conversations or big changes right now.

Yes, small steps are absolutely okay and often the safest, most sustainable way forward. Even small actions, like setting aside a few minutes for something calming or connecting briefly with someone you trust, can make a difference. We can choose one or two manageable things to try so you don’t feel overwhelmed. Would you like me to suggest some gentle options?
Yes, small steps feel more doable. I’m just so tired—big things feel impossible. A few gentle suggestions might help.

You might start with brief moments of grounding, like noticing five things you can see and five you can feel around you. Another gentle step could be writing down one thought or feeling each day without judging it, just to let it out. You could also plan a small, low-pressure interaction—like sending a short text to someone you trust. Which of these feels most doable for you right now?
I’m not sure about writing things down or texting someone. It might feel like more pressure. The grounding thing… I could maybe try that.

That’s a good choice—it’s low effort and can be done anywhere, and it helps bring you back to the present when your mind feels heavy. You can start with just a minute or two, noticing sights, textures, or sensations. There’s no “right” way—it’s simply about gently shifting your focus. Would you like me to walk you through it once so you know how it feels?
If you could walk me through it once, that might help. I’m not sure I’d do it right on my own.

Sure—let’s try it together now. Look around you and silently name five things you can see, like colors, objects, or shapes. Next, notice five things you can physically feel—your chair, the air on your skin, your feet on the floor. When you’re done, take one slow breath and see if you feel even a small shift.
I did it. It was… different. Not a fix, but I felt a bit more present, I think. Thank you for walking me through it.

I’m glad it gave you even a small sense of presence—that’s a meaningful start. These moments can build slowly over time, and practicing when you can may make that grounded feeling easier to access. You don’t have to aim for huge changes—small, steady steps can still ease the weight. Would you like to keep this as a daily tool?
I could try it when things feel too heavy. Not every day, maybe, but when I need it. It felt okay.

That sounds like a practical and compassionate approach—using it when you need it most can make it a reliable backup. Over time, you might notice it helps you find brief relief even during tough moments. Knowing you have something small you can control may bring a little stability. Would you like to explore one more gentle tool to keep in your back pocket?
I appreciate the help, but I don’t know if I have the energy for more right now. This one thing feels like enough to focus on.

That’s perfectly fine—sticking with one tool can keep things simple and manageable. It’s better to practice something that feels doable than to overload yourself with options. You can always add new strategies later if you feel ready. Would you like to talk a bit instead about how you’ve been feeling today?
I’ve been feeling… hollow. Like I’m going through motions I don’t care about. Even the things that used to matter—work, travel, stability—feel pointless now.

It sounds like life has lost its meaning for you right now, which can be deeply unsettling and draining. That hollow feeling often comes alongside grief or prolonged stress, making even familiar routines feel empty. If you’re open to it, we could explore what small moments or connections still hold even a faint spark for you. Would you like to look for those together?
I don’t know if I can look for sparks right now. It feels like too much. I just need to get through the day.

That’s okay—sometimes survival mode means focusing only on what gets you through the next hours. We can keep things very simple and practical, without pushing for meaning or big changes. Maybe grounding when you feel overwhelmed and giving yourself permission not to expect more is enough for now. Would that feel manageable today?
Yes, just getting through the day feels like enough. I’ll try the grounding thing if it gets too heavy. That feels manageable.

That sounds like a good plan—one step and one tool you can lean on when needed. Even small acts of care for yourself can help carry you through difficult days. If you notice the heaviness becoming too much, please consider reaching out to someone you trust or a crisis line. You deserve support, even in survival mode.
Thank you for listening. It helps just to say some of this out loud, without feeling like I have to fix it right away.

I’m glad you felt able to share—sometimes being heard without pressure can be its own kind of relief. You don’t have to solve everything at once for it to be worth talking about. This space is here for you whenever you need it. Would you like to check in again soon, just to keep that outlet open?
